Pathology + Clauses.question: ১) Usually Tuberculosis doesn't occur in Which of the following?
Pathology + Clauses.exp:
Tuberculosis (TB) can involve almost any organ, but some sites are characteristically rare. Thyroid gland TB is extremely rare because the thyroid is relatively resistant to Mycobacterium tuberculosis due to its rich blood supply, high iodine content, and other local protective factors.

TB can occur in:

  • Skin → Cutaneous tuberculosis

  • Intestine → Intestinal tuberculosis, commonly involving the ileocecal region

  • Brain → CNS TB, especially tuberculoma and tuberculous meningitis

High-yield TB recall:
Thyroid tuberculosis is exceptionally rare, despite TB being capable of affecting almost any organ.

Exam pearl:
TB can occur almost anywhere, but thyroid involvement is exceptionally uncommon.

Pathology + Clauses.question: ২) A granuloma surrounded by fibrous tissue that has undergone caseation necrosis, is called..?
Pathology + Clauses.exp:
A tubercle is the characteristic granulomatous lesion of tuberculosis. It consists of epithelioid cell granuloma with caseous necrosis, typically surrounded by Langhans giant cells and a rim of lymphocytes. With chronicity, fibrosis may develop around the lesion.

Why the others are incorrect:

  • Ghon's focus: A primary pulmonary TB lesion, usually a small subpleural focus of infection.

  • Ghon's complex: Ghon's focus + regional hilar lymph node involvement.

  • Hilar lymph node: A lymph node at the lung hilum; it may be involved in primary TB but is not itself called a tubercle.

High-yield TB recall:
Ghon complex = Ghon focus + ipsilateral hilar lymphadenopathy.

Exam pearl:
Caseating granuloma of TB = Tubercle.

Pathology + Clauses.question: ৩) XDR TB is resistant to which of the following drug?
Pathology + Clauses.exp:
XDR-TB (Extensively Drug-Resistant TB) is resistant to isoniazid (INH) and rifampicin (MDR-TB), plus a fluoroquinolone, with additional resistance to at least one key Group A drug depending on the current WHO definition.

So, among the given options, both INH + rifampicin and fluoroquinolones are involved.

Why other options are incorrect:

  • INH & rifampicin only: This defines MDR-TB, not XDR-TB.

  • Fluoroquinolone only: Insufficient for XDR-TB.

  • None: Incorrect.

High-yield TB recall:
MDR-TB = resistant to at least INH + rifampicin.
XDR-TB = MDR/RR-TB + fluoroquinolone resistance + additional resistance to a key Group A drug.

Exam pearl:
XDR-TB includes INH + rifampicin resistance AND fluoroquinolone resistance.

Pathology + Clauses.question: ৪) Route of administration of BCG vaccine is...?
Pathology + Clauses.exp:
Explanation: The BCG (Bacillus Calmette–Guérin) vaccine is administered by the intradermal (ID) route, usually over the left upper arm (deltoid region). It is a live attenuated vaccine used primarily to protect against severe forms of childhood tuberculosis, such as TB meningitis and miliary TB.

Why other options are incorrect:

  • I/V: Never used for BCG vaccination.

  • I/M: Incorrect route.

  • Subcutaneous: Not recommended because it increases the risk of local complications.

High-yield TB recall:

  • Route: Intradermal

  • Site: Left upper arm

  • Dose: 0.05 mL for neonates; 0.1 mL for older infants/children (program-dependent).

Exam pearl: BCG = Live attenuated vaccine given intradermally in the left upper arm.

Pathology + Clauses.question: ৫) Which is not a features of primary TB?
Pathology + Clauses.exp:
Primary TB occurs when a person is initially infected with Mycobacterium tuberculosis, usually through inhalation of infected droplets. Therefore, it represents an exogenous infection, not endogenous reactivation.

Typical features include:

  • Occurs commonly in children and previously unexposed individuals.

  • Subpleural primary lesion (Ghon focus), commonly in the lower part of the upper lobe or upper part of the lower lobe.

  • Ghon complex = Ghon focus + regional lymph node involvement.

Why the other options are correct features:

  • Occurs in children: Common in primary TB.

  • Subpleural lesion: Characteristic of the primary pulmonary focus.

  • Ghon's complex: Classic radiological/pathological feature of primary TB.

High-yield TB recall:
Primary TB = exogenous infection → Ghon focus → hilar lymph nodes → Ghon complex.

Exam pearl:
Primary TB is exogenous; secondary TB is usually endogenous reactivation.

Pathology + Clauses.question: ৬) Which is not true about Paratyphoid fever in relation to typhoid fever?
Pathology + Clauses.option2: course tends to be shorter and milder
Pathology + Clauses.option3: The rash may be more abundant
Pathology + Clauses.exp:
Paratyphoid fever is caused by Salmonella Paratyphi and is generally milder and shorter in duration than typhoid fever caused by S. Typhi.

Compared with typhoid fever:

  • Onset is often more abrupt.

  • Course is shorter and milder.

  • Rash may be more abundant.

  • Intestinal complications are less frequent, not more frequent.

Why the other options are true:

  • Abrupt onset: More characteristic of paratyphoid fever.

  • Shorter and milder course: Typical.

  • More abundant rash: Rose spots may be more numerous.

High-yield Enteric fever recall:
Paratyphoid = more abrupt onset + milder/shorter illness + more abundant rash + fewer intestinal complications.

Exam pearl:
Paratyphoid is generally milder than typhoid, with fewer intestinal complications.

Pathology + Clauses.question: ৭) Which giant cell is present in TB?
Pathology + Clauses.exp:
In tuberculosis, the granuloma characteristically contains Langhans giant cells, formed by the fusion of activated macrophages. They typically have nuclei arranged peripherally in a horseshoe/ring pattern.

Why the other options are incorrect:

  • Reed–Sternberg cell: Characteristic of Hodgkin lymphoma.

  • Langerhans cell: Antigen-presenting dendritic cell; associated with Langerhans cell histiocytosis.

  • Ghon's: Refers to the Ghon focus/complex in primary TB, not a giant cell.

High-yield TB recall:
TB granuloma = epithelioid cells + Langhans giant cells + caseous necrosis.

Exam pearl:
Langhans giant cell → Tuberculosis.

Pathology + Clauses.question: ৮) Which is not a first week symptom of enteric fever?
Pathology + Clauses.exp:
During the first week of enteric (typhoid) fever, patients commonly develop fever, headache, malaise, myalgia, and gastrointestinal symptoms. Constipation is more classically associated with the early stage of typhoid fever.

Diarrhoea is not a typical first-week symptom and is less characteristic overall, although it can occur, particularly in some cases.

Why the other options are less appropriate:

  • Myalgia: Common early systemic symptom.

  • Relative bradycardia: Can occur in typhoid fever (Faget sign).

  • Constipation: Classically described in the early phase of typhoid fever.

High-yield Enteric fever recall:
Early typhoid: gradually rising fever + headache + malaise + constipation; diarrhoea is less typical.

Exam pearl:
Think constipation rather than diarrhoea in early typhoid fever.

Pathology + Clauses.question: ৯) In case of enteric fever after a few days of bacteraemia the bacilli localized mainly in the lymphoid tissue of the
Pathology + Clauses.exp:
In enteric (typhoid) fever, Salmonella Typhi enters the bloodstream and subsequently localizes predominantly in the lymphoid tissue of the small intestine, especially the Peyer’s patches in the terminal ileum.

The organisms multiply within mononuclear phagocytes in Peyer’s patches, leading to enlargement, necrosis, and eventually ulceration.

Why the other options are incorrect:

  • Stomach: Not the primary site of localization.

  • Large intestine: May be involved secondarily, but not the main site.

  • Rectum: Not the characteristic site.

High-yield Enteric fever recall:
Typhoid → Peyer’s patches → terminal ileum → oval/longitudinal ulcers.

Exam pearl:
Salmonella Typhi primarily localizes in the Peyer’s patches of the terminal ileum.

Pathology + Clauses.question: ১০) Treatment of enteric fever should be continued for how many days?
Pathology + Clauses.exp:
Traditionally, enteric (typhoid) fever is treated for 14 days, particularly with chloramphenicol in classic textbook regimens.

However, the current duration depends on the antibiotic used and local resistance patterns. For example, uncomplicated typhoid may be treated with shorter courses of ceftriaxone or azithromycin in appropriate settings.

Why the other options are incorrect:

  • 5 days: Generally too short for the classic treatment regimen.

  • 7 days: May be adequate for some modern antibiotic regimens, but not the traditional standard.

  • 10 days: Used with some agents/regimens but not the classic textbook answer.

High-yield Enteric fever recall:
Classical exam answer: Typhoid fever treatment = 14 days.

Exam pearl:
For traditional MBBS MCQs, remember: Enteric fever → 14 days treatment.

Pathology + Clauses.question: ১১) Which is not a cause of false negative tuberculin test?
Pathology + Clauses.exp:
A false-negative tuberculin skin test (TST/Mantoux) occurs when a person infected with TB fails to mount an adequate delayed-type hypersensitivity response.

Important causes include:

  • Severe/disseminated TB → anergy may occur.

  • Extremes of age → reduced immune responsiveness.

  • Malnutrition → impaired cell-mediated immunity.

Previous BCG vaccination does not cause a false-negative TST. In fact, BCG vaccination can cause a false-positive TST, particularly when vaccination was recent.

Why the other options are incorrect:

  • Severe tuberculosis: Can cause anergy → false negative.

  • Extremes of age: Can reduce T-cell response → false negative.

  • Malnutrition: Impairs cell-mediated immunity → false negative.

High-yield TB recall:
False-negative TST causes: severe TB, extremes of age, malnutrition, immunosuppression, recent viral infection, and recent live-virus vaccination.

Exam pearl:
BCG vaccination → false-positive TST; severe TB/malnutrition → false-negative TST.

Pathology + Clauses.question: ১২) Which one is the most important diagnostic method in enteric fever?
Pathology + Clauses.exp:
Blood culture is the most important diagnostic test for enteric (typhoid) fever, particularly during the first week of illness, when bacteremia is most prominent. Isolation of Salmonella Typhi or S. Paratyphi from blood provides a definitive diagnosis.

Why the other options are incorrect:

  • Widal test: Has limited sensitivity and specificity; not preferred where reliable culture is available.

  • Urine culture: May become positive later but is less sensitive than blood culture.

  • CBC: May show leukopenia, but it is nonspecific and cannot confirm the diagnosis.

High-yield Enteric fever recall:
Blood culture → best diagnostic test, especially in the 1st week.
Stool culture → more useful later in the illness.

Exam pearl:
Suspected typhoid in the 1st week → Blood culture is the key diagnostic test.

Pathology + Clauses.question: ১৩) Which is not a component of Ghon's complex?
Pathology + Clauses.exp:
Ghon's complex is composed of:

  • Ghon's focus — primary pulmonary parenchymal lesion

  • Lymphangitis — lymphatic spread from the focus

  • Hilar lymphadenitis — involvement of regional hilar lymph nodes

Langhans giant cells are a histological component of the tuberculous granuloma, but they are not a component of Ghon's complex.

High-yield TB recall:
Ghon complex = Ghon focus + lymphangitis + hilar lymphadenitis.

Exam pearl:
Langhans giant cell belongs to the TB granuloma, not Ghon's complex.

Pathology + Clauses.question: ১৪) Which is the route of transmission for HEV?
Pathology + Clauses.exp:
Hepatitis E virus (HEV) is transmitted predominantly by the faecal–oral route, usually through ingestion of contaminated water or food. Outbreaks are particularly associated with poor sanitation.

Why the other options are incorrect:

  • Blood: Not the usual route, although transfusion-associated HEV transmission can rarely occur.

  • Sexual contact: Not the principal route of transmission.

  • Air droplets: HEV is not transmitted by respiratory droplets.

High-yield Hepatitis recall:
HAV and HEV → faecal–oral transmission.
HBV, HCV, HDV → predominantly blood/body-fluid transmission.

Exam pearl:
HEV = Faecal–oral → contaminated water → outbreaks.

Pathology + Clauses.question: ১৫) Which hepatotropic virus is called silent killer??
Pathology + Clauses.exp:
Hepatitis C (HCV) is classically called the “silent killer” because acute infection is often asymptomatic or minimally symptomatic, yet a significant proportion of infected individuals develop chronic hepatitis, which can progress to cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC).

Why the other options are incorrect:

  • HAV: Usually acute and self-limiting; does not cause chronic hepatitis.

  • HBV: Can cause chronic hepatitis and HCC, but the classic exam association “silent killer” = HCV.

  • HEV: Usually causes an acute, self-limiting infection; severe disease is particularly important in pregnancy.

High-yield Hepatitis recall:
HCV → often asymptomatic → chronic infection → cirrhosis → HCC.

Exam pearl:
HCV = “Silent killer” because chronic infection may remain clinically silent for years.

Pathology + Clauses.question: ১৬) Which is not a virulence factor for vibrio cholerae?
Pathology + Clauses.exp:
Important virulence factors of Vibrio cholerae include toxin-coregulated pilus (TCP) for intestinal adherence/colonization, cholera enterotoxin, and mucinase which facilitates penetration of the intestinal mucus layer.

Flagella primarily provide motility and are not considered a major virulence factor in the classic exam classification.

Why the other options are correct:

  • Pili (TCP): Essential for intestinal colonization and adherence.

  • Enterotoxin: Cholera toxin causes increased cAMP → chloride and water secretion → profuse watery diarrhoea.

  • Mucinase: Helps the organism penetrate the intestinal mucus layer.

High-yield Cholera recall:
TCP = colonization; Cholera toxin = watery diarrhoea; mucinase = mucus penetration.

Exam pearl:
V. cholerae virulence factors: TCP + cholera toxin + mucinase; flagella mainly provide motility.

Pathology + Clauses.question: ১৭) Which is not a feature of vibrio cholerae?
Pathology + Clauses.exp:
Vibrio cholerae is a curved, comma-shaped, Gram-negative bacillus, not a straight bacillus. It is highly motile due to a single polar flagellum and is oxidase positive.

Why the other options are correct:

  • Motile: Yes, due to its polar flagellum.

  • Single polar flagella: Characteristic feature.

  • Oxidase positive: A useful laboratory identification feature.

High-yield Vibrio cholerae recall:
Comma-shaped, Gram-negative, curved bacillus + single polar flagellum + oxidase positive.

Exam pearl:
Vibrio = “comma-shaped” bacillus, not a straight bacillus.

Pathology + Clauses.question: ১৮) Which one is causative organism for bacillary dysentery?
Pathology + Clauses.exp:
Bacillary dysentery is caused by Shigella species, especially Shigella dysenteriae. It is an invasive bacterial infection of the colon causing frequent small-volume stools containing blood and mucus, often accompanied by fever and abdominal cramps.

Why the other options are incorrect:

  • Entamoeba histolytica: Causes amoebic dysentery.

  • Giardia lamblia: Causes giardiasis, typically with greasy, foul-smelling diarrhoea and malabsorption.

  • Balantidium coli: Causes balantidial dysentery, which is uncommon.

High-yield Dysentery recall:
Bacillary dysentery → Shigella
Amoebic dysentery → Entamoeba histolytica

Exam pearl:
Shigella = classic causative organism of bacillary dysentery.

Pathology + Clauses.question: ১৯) Which is a microscopic feature of amoebic dysentery?
Pathology + Clauses.exp:
In amoebic dysentery, stool microscopy typically shows:

  • RBCs in clumps

  • Few pus cells, with eosinophils usually absent/scanty

  • Macrophages are few

  • Pyknotic bodies are present

Therefore, “Pyknotic bodies nil” is the incorrect feature.

Why the other options are correct:

  • RBC in clumps: Characteristic of amoebic dysentery.

  • Pus cells scanty: Usually fewer than in bacillary dysentery.

  • Very few macrophages: Can be seen.

  • Pyknotic bodies nil: Incorrect because pyknotic bodies may be present.

High-yield Amoebic dysentery recall:
Amoebic dysentery → clumped RBCs + relatively few pus cells + trophozoites containing ingested RBCs.

Exam pearl:
Entamoeba histolytica trophozoite containing ingested RBCs is the most important microscopic clue to amoebic dysentery.

Pathology + Clauses.question: ২০) Which is not a viral cause of acute watery diarrhoea?
Pathology + Clauses.exp:
The common viral causes of acute watery diarrhoea include Rotavirus, Norovirus, Adenovirus, and Astrovirus. “Archi virus” is not a recognized common viral cause of acute watery diarrhoea.

Why the other options are correct:

  • Rotavirus: Important cause of acute watery diarrhoea, especially in children.

  • Adenovirus: Enteric adenovirus can cause diarrhoea.

  • Astrovirus: Causes acute gastroenteritis, particularly in children.

High-yield Viral diarrhoea recall:
Rotavirus, Norovirus, Adenovirus, Astrovirus are important viral causes of acute gastroenteritis.

Exam pearl:
Acute watery diarrhoea → think Rotavirus, Norovirus, Adenovirus, Astrovirus.

Pathology + Clauses.question: ২১) ‘People who are involved in politics try to get power.’ - Here 'who are involved in politics' is-
Pathology + Clauses.exp:
“who are involved in politics” modifies the noun “People”, so it is an adjective (relative) clause.

  • People = noun being modified

  • who = relative pronoun

  • are involved in politics = predicate of the clause

The clause answers “Which people?” → People who are involved in politics.

Why the other options are incorrect:

  • Noun clause: Functions as a noun; this clause modifies people.

  • Adverbial clause: Modifies a verb, adjective, or adverb; this clause modifies a noun.

  • None: Incorrect because it is clearly an adjective clause.

High-yield Grammar recall:
A clause introduced by who, whom, whose, which, that that modifies a noun/pronoun is generally an adjective/relative clause.

Exam pearl:
“Who are involved in politics” modifies “People” → Adjective clause.

Pathology + Clauses.question: ২২) ‘I know the boy who went there.’ - In this sentence 'who went there' clause is a/an-
Pathology + Clauses.exp:
“who went there” modifies the noun “boy” and tells us which boy. Therefore, it is an adjective clause (relative clause).

  • I know the boy → Principal/independent clause

  • who went there → Adjective/relative clause

  • who → Relative pronoun

Why the other options are incorrect:

  • Noun clause: Does not function as a noun; it modifies boy.

  • Adverbial clause: Does not modify the verb know.

  • Principal clause: The principal clause is “I know the boy.”

High-yield Grammar recall:
A relative clause beginning with who/which/that and modifying a preceding noun is an adjective clause.

Exam pearl:
“Who went there” modifies “boy” → Adjective clause.

Pathology + Clauses.question: ২৩) ‘He asked me why I was late.’ - Here 'why I was late' clause is-
Pathology + Clauses.exp:
“why I was late” functions as the object of the verb “asked”. Since it performs the function of a noun, it is a noun clause.

  • He asked me → Principal clause

  • why I was late → Noun clause

  • why → Interrogative adverb introducing the noun clause

Why the other options are incorrect:

  • Principal clause: The principal clause is “He asked me.”

  • Adjective clause: It does not modify a noun.

  • Adverbial clause: It does not modify a verb/adjective/adverb by expressing time, reason, condition, etc.

High-yield Grammar recall:
A clause functioning as a subject, object, or complement is a noun clause.

Exam pearl:
“He asked me [why I was late]” → the bracketed clause is the object of “asked” → Noun clause.

Pathology + Clauses.question: ২৪) Identify the clause of the following sentence: ‘I took no notice of him, so he flew into rage.’ - Here 'so he flew into rage' clause is-
Pathology + Clauses.exp:
The sentence contains two independent clauses joined by the coordinating conjunction “so”:

  • I took no notice of him → Independent clause

  • so he flew into a rage → Coordinate clause

Here, “so” connects two clauses of equal grammatical status. Therefore, the second clause is a coordinate clause.

Why the other options are incorrect:

  • Noun clause: Does not function as a noun.

  • Adjective clause: Does not modify a noun/pronoun.

  • Adverbial clause: Although “so” indicates a result, in this construction it joins two independent clauses, making the second a coordinate clause.

High-yield Grammar recall:
Coordinating conjunctions: and, but, or, nor, for, so, yet (FANBOYS).

Exam pearl:
Two independent clauses joined by a coordinating conjunction → Coordinate clause.

Pathology + Clauses.question: ২৫) Identify the sentence with Adjective clause.
Pathology + Clauses.option2: He is the boy who come here yesterday
Pathology + Clauses.option3: The rumor, that she died, is not true
Pathology + Clauses.option4: She reads hard so that she can pass
Pathology + Clauses.exp:
The clause “who came here yesterday” modifies the noun “boy”. Therefore, it is an adjective (relative) clause.

  • who = relative pronoun

  • who came here yesterday → describes the boy

Why the other options are incorrect:

  • ক) I know what he said → Noun clause; “what he said” is the object of know.

  • গ) The rumor, that she died, is not true → Noun clause functioning in apposition to “the rumor” (though the punctuation/construction is nonstandard).

  • ঘ) She reads hard so that she can pass → Adverbial clause of purpose.

High-yield Grammar recall:
A clause that modifies or describes a noun/pronoun is an adjective clause.

Exam pearl:
who/which/that + modifies a noun → Adjective clause.
